metadata.note: The Syracuse, Geneva and Corning main line -- 57 miles down the west side of Seneca Lake, and the line the Penn Yan branch was built to reach. Chartered Aug 27 1875, opened Dec 10 1877, it tied the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western at Corning to the New York Central and the Lehigh Valley at Geneva and opened a path from the Finger Lakes to the Pennsylvania coal fields. From 1881 the Fall Brook Coal Company leased and worked it for twenty years as the northern end of a roughly 250-mile system running from Williamsport, Pennsylvania to Lyons, New York, with through passenger service over the Geneva and Lyons, this line and the Pine Creek Railway. It absorbed the Penn Yan and New York Railroad on Oct 1 1885, was leased to the New York Central and Hudson River in 1899, merged with the Geneva, Corning and Southern in 1909 and into the New York Central in 1914, and was thereafter the Fall Brook Subdivision of the Central's Pennsylvania Division. Norfolk Southern runs it today as the Corning Secondary, freight only, with the Finger Lakes Railway holding trackage rights from Geneva to Himrod Junction. See penn_yan_and_new_york_railway.geojson for the Dresden branch, which meets this line at Dresden.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: THE BIG ONE: no date has been found for when passenger service on the Geneva-Corning line ended. Five separate searches across Wikipedia, Railpace, Crooked Lake Review, the Fall Brook Railway site and Geneva local history turned up the corporate chronology in detail and nothing at all on the end of passenger trains. Because this map draws passenger service only, the last feature is stopped at the 1914 merger into the New York Central -- a hard corporate date through which passenger service demonstrably ran -- rather than being carried forward to a guessed end year. The line therefore UNDER-states its passenger history and will disappear from the map decades too early; anyone with an Official Guide or a NYC Pennsylvania Division timetable can extend the final segment. Also unsourced: every headway and speed here; the opening dates of individual sections between Corning and Geneva, only the 1877 completion being documented; and the station list, so the stops named in the line labels are the towns the trace passes rather than a confirmed timetable list. The 57.76-mile and 6.43-mile figures are quoted at second hand from Poor's Manual rather than read in the original.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: Chartered Aug 27 1875 and completed Corning to Geneva in 1877 after long argument with the property owners on South Main Street in Geneva; the road opened Dec 10 1877 and the first trains ran that December. It linked the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western at Corning with the New York Central and the Lehigh Valley at Geneva, and gave Geneva a route to the Pennsylvania coal fields. segments.note: Leased to and operated by the Fall Brook Coal Company for twenty years from 1881, becoming the northern link in a system that ran some 250 miles from Williamsport, Pennsylvania to Lyons, New York. The Fall Brook offered through passenger service Lyons to Williamsport over the Geneva and Lyons, this line, and the Pine Creek Railway. On Oct 1 1885 the Penn Yan and New York Railroad was consolidated into the company, which kept its own name -- that branch is drawn in penn_yan_and_new_york_railway.geojson and joins this line at Dresden.
